title: LBMA Precious Metals market volumes, June-August 2026, and their significance
author: StoneX
description: Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery. Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Precious metals experienced three distinct phases during June-August 2026: early weakness, summer consolidation, and a strong recovery in August. Silver remained the strongest performer, gaining approximately 159% over the previous year. ETF holdings increased and speculative long positions expanded significantly during August, reflecting renewed investor confidence. Options volumes nearly doubled compared to the same period in 2025, highlighting increased hedging and speculative activity. The LBMA precious metals market between June and August 2026 was defined by a transition from correction to recovery. Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery. Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain Rhona O’Connell, StoneX Financial Ltd; 4 th September May 2026 Any views expressed here are of the writer and do not reflect a house view from NASDAQ. Welcome to our monthly round-up of the LBMA OTC trading volumes in gold, silver, platinum and palladium, as recorded on a daily basis by the Association. These are split into spot, swap/forward, options and LoanLeaseDeposit (LLD) and give a flavour of the markets’ activity and how they were influenced by external forces and news items. Due to technical issues plus some holiday leave, this piece looks back at the June-August this year against June-August 2025 All references to COMEX or NYMEX positioning refer to Managed Money, not commercial positions. General introduction: Daily June-August average compared with daily average for the equivalent period in 2025. Source: LBMA Source: LBMA, StoneX Colour coding ranks the metals against each other in each sector June to August was a particularly eventful period for the precious complex, with the intersection of a hawkish new Fed, an interventionist Treasury, a re-escalating Gulf war, and a structurally weak dollar. Gold, silver, platinum and palladium, September 2025 to early September 2026 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver still the outperformer at +159%; Platinum 125%, Gold 124% and palladium, 118% The three key drivers overall included the vicissitudes of the Gulf war, a dollar that was weak against the euro while strong against the yen – although it could be argued that the yen was independently weak - and a virtual tug-of-war developed between Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen, which is particularly relevant for gold. By the end of the period, the dollar-debasement argument, which had been fading, reasserted itself. After the rally in May, especially in silver, all four metals drifted lower through June and July as the summer doldrums set in and once again some major players were unwilling to take strategic positions. The dollar strengthened in June during the ceasefire in the Gulf but once escalation had resumed the currency entered a downward path that only paused for breath in late August. The metals did rally in late June as the Gulf ceasefire failed, with reciprocal strikes between the US and Iran raising new doubts over the return of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. As we write in early September those doubts have still not been dispelled. In the background it was interesting to see the rising correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield, but not that surprising since they are both rooted around the Gulf conflict and by definition gold forms part of this matrix also. Growing correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield since the onset of hostilities Source: Bloomberg, StoneX January 2025 – early September2026 spot volumes, tonnes Gold Silver Source: for all charts above; LBMA, StoneX Platinum Palladium COMEX, NYMEX, positioning to 25 th August 2026 GOLD SILVER PLATINUM PALLADIUM Source: CFTC, StoneX Gold Gold sold off hard in June then spent July trading around $4,100 and occasionally dipping toward $4,000 in one interesting development, gold opened lower on July 13 and fell further despite the US–Iran airstrikes over that weekend, a telling sign that the hawkish-Fed/yield story was overriding the geopolitical safe-haven bid at that point. From a mid-July trough just below$4,000, the metal then staged its best stretch of the year, rallying: by 18% from its mid-July low to an intraday high of $4,696 on August 25 th , its highest since mid-May, before snapping a five-day winning streak late in the month after US inflation data came in above target, then steadying near $4,400–$4,600 into month-end. That mid-August week was gold's best since January, and gold-mining stocks had their hottest five-day run since 2008. Inverted gold and the real two-year yield Source: Bloomberg, StoneX It may seem counter-intuitive that gold prices were rising in the face of continuing increases in bond yields, but this is explained as follows. Yields were rising on inflation and fiscal fears rather than growth; a widening fiscal deficit, inflation persistently above 2% (for 65 months above target as Keviin Warsh noted in his Jackson Hole presentation at end-August), a weaker dollar, and an avalanche of corporate bond issuance to fund AI and data-centre build-outs — which is precisely an environment in which gold can flourish. Second, and probably more significantly, the Treasury Secretary’s efforts to suppress yields via FX intervention (something which almost invariably fails) were seen by the markets as an effort at fiscal dominance and financial repression: an admission that the debt load could no longer tolerate market-clearing rates. Sure enough, by early September 30-year yields were back over 5.2%. The US 5Y-30Y curve; long-term Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Adding to gold’s August rally were soft inflation numbers, but not soft enough for the Fed and Mr Warsh’s Jackson Hole comments were visibly more hawkish than the post-FOMC Press conferences held previously. Trading activity Turnover, M ounces Source: NASDAQ, LBMA As far as market turnover is concerned, the sell-off in early June was in the heaviest volume of the period, with over 30M ounces traded on each of three consecutive days. The rest of June was relatively busy but turnover in July was paltry. After some improvement in early August, the 5 th was particularly heavy as optimism grew over the possibility of Hormuz being reopened and with hedge funds getting on board gold rallied from $4,066 to $4,268, laying the foundations for consolidation in a new range, and latterly for the rally to almost $4,700 at month-end. That rally was in relatively thin conditions until the high-volume sell-off on the 28 th in the wake of Kevin Warsh’s comments. Gold from September 2025 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Among the OTC derivative sectors, swaps/forwards were sluggish in June until towards month-end when, after falling below the 10-day moving average, forward activity picked up and helped to drive the price to the low for the period ($3,943 intraday). Activity increased in July and on more than one occasion seemed to be related to technical indicators, notably the moving averages. This was mirrored to an extent in the LLD segment, notably in early mid-July where heavy activity around $4,100 suggests that there was some supply-side hedging going through the market as prices failed at this level. As LLD volumes drifted off, the path higher became easier and indeed there was only one LLD trading day in August and that came on the 5th, quelling an initial attempt to clear $4,400. Volumes were high in mid-late July, with prices moving sideways, suggesting good two-way activity. After a busy day early in August, with a failed assault on $4,400, swaps/forwards tailed off. Finally the options market the volume over the period was almost double that of June-August 2025, with a daily average of almost 1.1M ounces. Even so, volumes were sluggish in June and July. The stand-out day, with 4.9M ounces going through was again 5 th August, along with high volumes in spot and swaps/forwards, suggesting that part of that swollen volume was hedging against options exposure. This was on that same day when the market rallied off the 20-day moving average at $4065 to $4,268; i.e. the 5 th when on hopes that Hormuz would reopen. Over the period the ETF gold holdings opened at 4,121t, briefly continued the decline that had started in mid-May, but then turned higher to close Augst at 4,181t, a net year-to-date gain of 156t. CFTC figures show outright Managed money longs rising from 402t to 497t on 25 th August, while outright shorts fluctuated from 54t to 64t the following week, fluctuated around 50t for much of the rest of the period before short covering into 23t in early Augst ; they closed the period higher again, at 47t. Gold and the S&P (log-scales) Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver As usual, silver was the highest-beta play on the same macro forces outlined above, and once again it moved violently. After a January record near $121–$122, it had already halved by early summer, opening June at $74 before a two-leg tumble to $56 on the 24 th , and entering a five-week period in a sideways trend between$55 and $63. This set the scene for the August recovery, with silver reaching an intraday high of &1 on the 28 th before, with gold, going into reverse post-Warsh. Gold and silver action, correlation Source: Bloomberg As well as the major factors that drove gold and by association, silver, the latter metal also has its industrial character to address, given that 70% of silver fabrication (ex-investment) is in industrial uses. The June-quarter hawkish Fed hold at 3.50–3.75% and a divided committee hit silver's industrial engine directly, and the gold-silver ratio widened from a May low near 55:1 to about 69:1 by mid-July — a classic sign of silver underperforming gold in a risk-off environment. The same soft-data/weak-dollar cocktail that lifted gold then drove the August rebound, amplified by silver's leverage. The August rally was accompanied, and to some extent driven by, the return of Managed Monay longs (after quite an exodus earlier in the year), rising from 2,822t in mid-July to 3,444t in late August, while shorts were slower to respond, having continued to expand to 1,368t in mid-August (from 941t in mid-July) then contracting to 1,143t in late August. Gold:silver ratio Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Although the US economy is relatively resilient and the onset of AI, vehicle electrification and solar cells will combine to take silver into an expanding pre-investment deficit, in the immediate term these forces are muffled to a degree with the current surplus of solar cells (and a minor threat from copper) while the ebbs and flows of vehicle electrification are a matter of record – although this is more relevant to the PGM than to silver; see below. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Spot volumes were down 39% over the period compared with June-August 2025. With the exception of 5 th August, much mentioned in our gold comments (Hormuz hopes), silver’s spot volume fluctuations were similar to those of gold with high volume in the June retreat (thus making the market less crowded) and then a sluggish period through to mid-July. As prices stabilised spot activity cautiously increased, although volumes in the rally to $70, which was reached on 21 st August, were patchy. On the 21 st , volumes were much livelier. As hedging activity developed (increased volumes in swaps/forwards and options also) and called a halt to the rally. After three successive efforts to clear $70, the market capitulated and the sharp fall to $66 on the 28 th was in heavy spot volume (but not in the derivatives). Derivatives activity was heavy in June in swaps and forwards, which will certainly have been instrumental in the price fall and would to some extent have been self-fulfilling. The LLD segment was 25% down on the 2025 equivalent and here, too , was busiest in the June fall. There was some cautious interest in mid-August when silver was flirting with $65, suggesting some hedging, especially as the price didn’t clear that level at that stage. Finally there was activity at month-end as silver was again on the retreat. Platinum and palladium Platinum was the "cleanest" fundamental story of the four, driven more by physical scarcity than by the dollar. The market is expected to be in deficit for the fourth consecutive year this year, despite expected falls in auto and jewellery demand, while supply is likely to be broadly steady. South Africa accounts for roughly 72% of refined production, and that concentration was the summer's active risk. National primary output fell from about 5.3 million ounces in 2006 to roughly 3.9 million in 2025 and while looking steady this year it is expected to decline again next year. On the demand side, the hydrogen fuel-cell demand, while coming from a very low base, adds a new industrial floor. Palladium trades heavily on autos (80% of demand comes from catalytic converters in gasoline and hybrid vehicles) so it is exposed to two secular headwinds; platinum substitution and the rise of battery-electric vehicles. The June price softness reflected slower automaker procurement, soft electronics demand, caution in the jewellery sector, plus almost non-existent investment, while supply was steady. The July bounce was seasonal restocking rather than scarcity. The one genuine supply-side tail risk remains geopolitical — Russia is the world's largest palladium producer (nickel by-product), followed by South Africa (platinum by-product) so any escalation of sanctions on Russian metal would be the scenario that could override the surplus narrative, much as it did in 2022. This is still up in the air. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Platinum spot turnover was 49% down on the equivalent period of 2025, while options and LLD were both down by ~20%. Swaps/forwards were the only sector in the black, up by 21%. Trading volumes were choppy, with a couple of heavy days trading in spot in the first week as prices came extended a slide from $1,980 ,although this was not mirrored in the OTC derivatives. The sharp fall from $1,906 to $1,772 was one of those days, and Spot volumes dwindled thereafter as prices slid to $1,535 on 1st July. At this point spot and forwards kicked in, in a classic surge in volume in a price reversal and suggesting industrial forward buying, sparking a period of price consolidation, during which the only point of interest was heavy forward activity on the approach to $1,700, which failed, implying continued industrial interest and quite possibly inventory management. Early August saw heavy volumes in spot forwards and options as prices surged from $1,629 to$1,751, stemming from a second day of oil price declines and a weaker dollar (Gulf again), taking all the metals higher and precipitating a change of range. After a period of consolidation the rally to a four-time failed test of $1,900 enjoyed good volumes in everything except options and the reversal saw strong spot activity, suggesting profit taking / stale bull liquidation. Platinum, palladium and the ratio, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Palladium prices moved closely in line with platinum over the period, with the correlation between the two not dropping below 0.84, and reaching 0.90 on occasion. Spot trading patterns were not that similar, however, with the early June fall being more of a thin volume slide. There was some intermittent interest in late July in both spot and forwards as the market started to benefit from its prior period of price consolidation, and setting the scene for the sharp jump in early August that had affected all four metals. Forwards were busy in late July on the approach to $1,300, while there was little options activity until mid-August as prices completed a bear move from the failure at $1,400. That failure had itself been accompanied by heavy LLD volume, suggesting some hedging activity. Platinum, palladium and the spread, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX

title: The Value of Data Becomes Even More Important in an AI-Powered Financial System
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Nasdaq's latest whitepaper, Unlocking Financial Markets: Understanding the Role of Data in a Digital Economy, examines how data powers modern capital markets and why trusted information has become one of the most important forms of financial infrastructure.
content: The financial industry is entering another period of profound transformation. The first major shift moved markets from crowded trading floors to electronic infrastructure. The next is already underway. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how decisions are made. Trading is becoming increasingly automated. Market participants are preparing for always-on markets, faster settlement cycles, and new forms of digital infrastructure. Together, these developments point toward a future that is faster, more interconnected, and increasingly dependent on data. That reality sits at the center of Nasdaq's latest whitepaper, Unlocking Financial Markets: Understanding the Role of Data in a Digital Economy , which examines how data powers modern capital markets and why trusted information has become one of the most important forms of financial infrastructure. While conversations about financial data often focus on cost, the paper argues that a more important question is value. "Data is the foundation of every modern financial decision," said Brandon Tepper, Senior Vice President and Global Head of Data for Nasdaq's Capital Access Platforms. "As markets become more automated and AI-enabled, the quality and integrity of the data underneath those decisions becomes increasingly important." Building the Financial Data Stack The financial ecosystem relies on a broad range of information sources. At the base is exchange market data, which provides a transparent view of regulated market activity and serves as the foundation for price discovery. Above that layer sits a growing ecosystem of complementary and alternative data products, including indices, analytics, research, news, and other datasets that help firms generate additional insight. This layered structure has expanded dramatically over the past decade as firms seek new ways to analyze markets, manage risk, and uncover opportunities. Global spending on financial market data surpassed $50 billion in 2025, reflecting growing demand for increasingly sophisticated datasets and analytical tools. Yet the paper finds that the value created throughout the broader ecosystem ultimately depends on the quality and integrity of the foundational layer beneath it. Exchange data serves as the common reference point against which other datasets, analytics, and models are built and validated. A useful way to think about the relationship is through infrastructure. New applications, analytics tools, and AI models may represent the visible innovations attracting attention across the industry, but they depend on an underlying foundation that must remain reliable, resilient, and universally trusted. Why AI Raises the Stakes The growing adoption of artificial intelligence is amplifying the importance of high-quality financial data. AI systems can identify patterns, generate predictions, and automate decisions, but they do not independently determine what is true. Their outputs are only as reliable as the data on which they are trained, tested, and governed. As a result, trusted exchange market data plays a critical role as both a training and validation layer for AI-enabled finance. Standardized, transparent, and auditable market information helps ensure that models remain anchored to observable market outcomes rather than incomplete, fragmented, or unverified signals. This becomes increasingly important as firms deploy AI across portfolio management, trading, risk management, surveillance, compliance, and investment research. In more automated environments, errors can be propagated at greater speed and scale, increasing the importance of maintaining trusted sources of market truth. The paper argues that AI is not reducing the importance of exchange data. Instead, it is increasing demand for the trusted reference layer that allows firms to evaluate models, measure performance, and manage risk with confidence. Preparing for an Always-On Future Artificial intelligence is only one part of a broader evolution underway across financial markets. Industry initiatives ranging from extended trading hours and accelerated settlement to the growing use of digital assets and on-chain infrastructure are creating a financial system that operates with greater speed and continuity than ever before. In that environment, trusted data becomes even more essential. Risk systems require accurate information. Automated workflows require reliable inputs. Smart contracts and digital infrastructure still depend on trusted reference prices that connect automated actions to real-world market value. As the financial system becomes more interconnected, the importance of maintaining a transparent, standardized, and continuously available foundation of market data only grows. "The future financial system will undoubtedly introduce new technologies and new capabilities," Tepper said. "But innovation doesn't eliminate the need for trusted information. If anything, it increases the importance of having a shared source of truth that market participants can rely on." The Foundation of Future Innovation Innovation across financial services continues to accelerate. New data products, analytics platforms, AI workflows, and investment tools are creating significant value throughout the industry. But the research suggests that the success of those innovations remains closely linked to the integrity of the underlying market information from which they derive value. As markets move toward a future defined by greater automation, more continuous trading, and increasingly sophisticated technologies, maintaining trusted market data is not simply a market structure consideration. It is fundamental to preserving transparency, confidence, and innovation across the financial system. And in a world increasingly shaped by AI, the value of data may ultimately be measured not by the insights it generates, but by the trust it enables. title: What is Driving Free Cash Flow Yield Performance in Japan?
author: Johnny Chen
description: Free cash flow is the cash a company has left after paying for its operations and investments. Free cash flow ETFs first appeared in the United States in 2016 and began expanding into the APAC region in 2023. This study examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns. Because free cash flow yield puts price in the denominator, high free cash flow yield is easily linked to low valuation. The free cash flow component (FCF/B) has demonstrated a steady upward trend over the period from May 2007 through June 2026 Beyond answering the value question, this points to a further possibility worth exploring: FCF/B on its own may be a viable building block for a free cash flow strategy in Japan. Free cash flow is the cash a company has left after paying for its operations and investments. Free cash flow ETFs first appeared in the United States in 2016 and began expanding into the APAC region in 2023. This study examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns. The Rise of Free Cash Flow Strategies in APAC The free cash flow strategy gained significant momentum in APAC recently, with total 35 free cash flow ETFs have been launched in China, Hong Kong, Japan and Korea between 1 January 2023 and 30 June 2026. Chart 1 shows that two newly listed free cash flow ETFs in Japan, each with more than one year of performance history, Global X MSCI Japan Cash Flow Kings ETF 234A and Global X S&P 500 Cash Flow Top 100 ETF (356A) , have delivered one-year total returns of 40% and 33%, as of 30 June 2026. Chart 1: The Launch Trend of Free Cash Flow ETFs Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Product Intelligence Japan Cash Flow ETF 234A invests in the universe of top 500 large and mid-cap Japanese stocks and is constructed by selecting the 50 stocks with the highest free cash flow yield from the universe. We are interested in whether this free cash flow yield strategy can deliver long-term outperformance and what drives its returns. Examining Long-Term Historical Performance and Value Exposure ETF 234A is a newly launched product with limited history, so we use its underlying index of this ETF to represent the long-term performance of free cash flow yield in Japan. TOPIX 500 index is used as market benchmark because the underlying index is also using the top 500 large and mid-cap as universe. Chart 2 shows that since May 2007, the underlying index of this ETF has delivered an annualized total return of 8.6%, while TOPIX 500 has delivered only 2.6%. This suggests that free cash flow yield in Japan not only generated strong one-year performance (40%) but also outperformed the benchmark from 31 May 2007 to 30 June 2026. The price denominator in free cash flow yield (free cash flow per share divided by stock price) from ETF 234A shares the same denominator as value factor (book value divided by stock price) of TOPIX 500 value index. The TOPIX 500 value index has surged since 2023 following the launch of Japan value program which is a Tokyo stock exchange initiative that encourages Japanese companies, particularly those with low share prices relative to their assets to use capital more efficiently, improve profitability, and better reward shareholders. Compared with the TOPIX 500 value Index, the underlying index of ETF 234A has exhibited a similar surge in returns since 2023, as shown in Chart 2. Therefore, we would like to determine whether the returns based on free cash flow yield are driven by the value factor. Chart 2: Japan Cash Flow Kings ETF 234A Index Performance vs Benchmarks Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Index Research & Development Looking Inside Free Cash Flow Yield 1) A Factor Lens: Value Matters, so Do Quality and Investment Factors We applied Fama-French five factor model, which is a model that explains asset returns using multiple risk factors rather than just the market, on the underlying index of ETF 234A and TOPIX 500. The model result shown in Chart 3 indicates a higher coefficient and statistically significant exposure to the value factor whereas TOPIX 500’s exposure to value is limited. In 2025, the value factor was associated with the underlying index of ETF 234A 1-year 30% return by adding 7.6 points, which is about 25% of the total return. Overall, the model suggests that the underlying index combines large-cap, value with additional tilts toward companies earning strong profits (high quality) and conservative investing. Chart 3: Output of Fama-French 5 Factor Model Source: Fama-French Model, Nasdaq Index Research & Development 2) Separating Cash-Flow Strength from Valuation for Regression Decomposition Given that free cash flow yield uses stock price in the denominator, a natural question is whether high free cash flow yield companies largely overlap with low-valuation names, and therefore exhibit high exposure to the value factor. More importantly, to what extent is the observed performance of the “free cash flow yield” explained by this value exposure? To address this question, we decompose free cash flow yield by expressing it as Free Cash Flow Per Share / Price = Free Cash Flow Per Share / Book Value (free cash flow component) × Book Value / Price (value component). We then applied the return decomposition framework below to regress the daily returns of the high free cash flow yield portfolio on the TOPIX 500 market return, the free cash flow‑to‑book value return premium, and the book value-to-price premium. This approach allows us to separate the return contributions from the overall market, the free cash flow component, and the value component. Note: The high free cash flow yield portfolio on the left hand side was constructed by selecting the top 250 high free cash flow yield stocks from the top 500 large‑ and mid‑cap universe in Japan. The return premium on the right hand side were constructed using the same methodology as the high free cash flow yield portfolio. The regression results indicate that the high free cash flow yield portfolio’s returns may be driven by market, while both free cash flow‑to‑book value and book value-to-price provide additional independent explanatory power with t-stat 9.57 and 8.93 respectively. Both the free cash flow‑to‑book value and book value-to-price premiums are statistically significant (at the 1% level), not just one. This shows that the free cash flow‑to‑book value component contributes to returns independently of value, beyond the shared price denominator. 3) Interaction Between Free Cash Flow-to-Book and Value Component After showing that both free cash flow‑to‑book value and book‑to‑price are important in explaining returns, the next step is to see whether they interact with each other. In other words, do companies with high free cash flow‑to‑book value behave like traditional value stocks (high book value‑to‑price), or are they different? Looking at the TOPIX 500, if we divide the 500 stocks into high and low groups based on their free cash flow component and value component separately, only one-third of the high free cash flow-to-book stocks also belong to high value group, which indicates that free cash flow and value are capturing different names from the universe. Chart 4 shows the backtested relative performance of each metric, constructed as the high-metric group index divided by the low-metric group. The free cash flow yield (Top 500 FCF/P) tracks the free cash flow component (Top 500 FCF/B) closely, both delivering steady gains. The value component (Top 500 B/P) follows a different path. It led from 2021 to early 2026 but gave back much of that gain over the past four months and saw larger drawdowns throughout. In short, free cash flow yield behaves more like the free cash flow component than like value. Chart 4: Free Cash Flow‑to‑Book Value and Book Value-to-Price Return Premium Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Index Research & Development Conclusion Because free cash flow yield puts price in the denominator, high free cash flow yield is easily linked to low valuation. But our factor attribution and regression analysis show the free cash flow component has explanatory power beyond value. Furthermore, when decomposing free cash flow yield into its free cash flow and value components, we found that not only is the constituent overlap between the high free cash flow component group and the value group relatively low, but the two groups have also exhibited distinct return patterns. Compared with the existing free cash flow yield methodology used by ETF 234A, the free cash flow component (FCF/B) has demonstrated a steady upward trend over the period from May 2007 through June 2026. Beyond answering the value question, this points to a further possibility worth exploring: FCF/B on its own may be a viable building block for a free cash flow strategy in Japan. title: Chartstopper: September 4, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: The two big themes this week were the rate path for the Federal Reserve and the Iran conflict.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Fed rate path in focus as Waller signals patience August jobs report blows past expectations, lifting hike odds Iran conflict pushes oil back above $90 AVGO caps a blockbuster earnings season Markets finish flat as inflation concerns offset strong earnings This Week The two big themes this week were the rate path for the Federal Reserve and the Iran conflict. For the Fed, there were two notable developments: Fed Governor Chris Waller said he was open to leaving rates unchanged if recent disinflation continues, or, as he put it, “to paraphrase John Lennon… give disinflation a chance.” The economy added 162,000 jobs in August, supporting Chair Kevin Warsh’s view last Friday that inflation is the Fed’s focus . That job gain was nearly triple expectations for 55,000 jobs added, and the previous two months were revised up, flipping July’s job change into positive territory. So, in the last week, market expectations for Fed hikes this year have increased to nearly 40 basis points (bp) from under 30bp. Of course, the Iran conflict isn’t doing the Fed any favors on the inflation front. In the last week, U.S. oil prices are up over $5 to move back above $90 per barrel – near three-month highs. That’s because hopes for any kind of near-term ceasefire seem increasingly remote after the U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes and more oil tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. There were also reports that the Trump administration would not accept a return to the expired Memorandum of Understanding and would require an agreement covering both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program. Elsewhere, second-quarter earnings season wrapped up with mega-cap AVGO beating earnings estimates with nearly 100% per annum (p.a.) growth, helping the Nasdaq-100® finish the quarter with almost 80% p.a. earnings growth. Despite the (very) strong earnings growth, concerns about inflation and rate hikes weighed on markets with the Nasdaq-100® finishing the week flat, while 10-year Treasury yields are up about 5bp to 4.8%. title: Biweekly Investment Insights: When hawks fly, stay grounded in the fundamentals
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: Markets have turned more cautious following a hawkish Fed message, rising Treasury yields, and trade tensions. While higher rates may pressure equities near term, earnings expectations remain the stronger driver of Nasdaq-100 performance.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Macro & micro square off (again) as investors move past Q2 earnings season Fed Chair Warsh delivered a hawkish speech at Jackson Hole focused on battling inflation Despite government intervention, Treasury yields have rerated higher U.S. corporate earnings strength & credit spreads still point to a constructive backdrop Biweekly Charts in Focus: Rising Treasury yields can dampen market sentiment, but next 12-month consensus EPS have a stronger historical relationship with equity index returns Source: Bloomberg. As of August 31, 2026, monthly basis. Source: Bloomberg. As of August 31, 2026, monthly basis. Summary The end of a strong Q2 earnings season coincided with August NFPs that were notably above estimates and a decisively hawkish message from Federal Reserve Chair Warsh at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium on August 28 th : “Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job.” After the recent downshift in the market pricing of Fed rate hike expectations through 2026, they have reset higher as have Treasury yields. Higher Treasury yields typically impact equities via a higher risk-free rate which can reduce the present value of future cash flows and compress equity valuations, all else being equal. They can also tighten financial conditions which dampens risk appetite. However, per our Biweekly Charts in Focus, over the past 20 years, annual changes in Treasury 10-year yields cannot effectively predict YoY changes to the Nasdaq-100. It is the fundamentals such as earnings expectations—measured here by the annual change in Nasdaq-100 NTM consensus EPS—which historically have had greater explanatory power in terms of equity index returns. The markets and the economy have lived with higher rates in the past, and the Treasury 10-year yield matches up directionally with U.S. nominal GDP growth since 1980. As we’ve discussed before , it is not just the rise in rates but it is also why rates are rising which is important. Our decomposition model of nominal Treasury 10-year yield changes YTD continues to point to it being overwhelmingly driven by the change in real rates as a byproduct of Fed policy repricing amidst a resilient U.S. economy. Against this backdrop and amidst shifting equity market returns, corporate earnings and revenue estimates remain solid over the next few quarters. But we are watching to see if lower expectations develop into mid-2027. The strong corporate earnings construct is also reflected in U.S. corporate credit spreads which are hovering near 20-year tights. In the very near-term, as the markets push into what has historically been the weakest month for U.S. equity returns (September), equities could remain unsettled amidst the higher rates backdrop, AI capex questions, and ahead of key macro data points that will further inform the September 16 th Fed meeting. Details Hawkish Warsh commentary & higher Treasury yields Fed Chair Warsh’s speech at Jackson Hole was more in-line with the recent tilt of the FOMC in terms of looking to combat inflation sooner than later. Despite better-than-expected PCE and CPI readings recently, he stressed that “they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” He also noted that “on balance, I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.” Warsh’s latest comments and stronger August NFPs of 162,000 (above consensus of 55,000), along with the two prior months revised higher by a net of 55,000 jobs, sent another reverberation through the market pricing of Fed rate hike expectations. We admit that we show Figure 3 frequently. While it speaks to the evolving market narrative, it is also a reminder that it is important for investors to remain strategically disciplined, and to focus on the health of corporate fundamentals as well as the structural growth stories amidst the macro volatility [ 1 ] . The combination of a broadly resilient U.S. economy, sticky inflation trends and resurgent energy prices, ongoing U.S. fiscal concerns, the market navigating an evolving Fed communications strategy, and the battle for capital globally between governments and AI-related corporate debt (Goldman Sachs estimates nearly $500 billion of AI-related corporate debt issuance in 2026 YTD), has pushed the long-end of the yield curve higher. Figure 3: Number of 25bp hikes priced in by Fed meeting has round-tripped last 3 weeks Source: Bloomberg Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the long-end liquidity buyback program will at least double, raising the per-operation cap from $2 billion to at least $4 billion for 10-, 20-, and 30-year debt effective September 9 th , with the Treasury General Account potentially tapped to fund the operations rather than issuing additional front-end bills. However, 10-year yields are now higher by more than 10 basis points from when Secretary Bessent announced these measures on August 19 th . So, is the Treasury 10-year yield at its highest since January 2025 out of sync with the fundamentals? With nominal U.S. GDP running at 6.6% YoY, as Figure 4 shows, a 10-year yield of around 4.75% does not seem out of bounds (all else being equal given the various dynamics at play such as term premium, inflation dynamics, etc.). A lender extending 10-year credit to the U.S. government would expect, at minimum, to be compensated for the opportunity cost of capital—which is roughly what the economy can generate in nominal terms. Figure 4: Treasury 10-year yields track directionally with U.S. nominal GDP Source: Bloomberg Shifting equity returns & flows Taking a step back, while macro clouds have gathered (again), we continue to note the broadening of equity returns beneath the index levels. As a proxy for the growth versus value trade, as well as for AI enablers versus AI adopters, Figure 5 shows the massive outperformance of semis relative to banks on a 6-month rolling basis—a +4.1 standard deviation move versus the 10-year average as of mid-June 2026. However, banks recovered on a relative basis on the back of strong earnings and a broadly resilient U.S. economy while semis sold off notably in July (SOX was -20.6%, its largest monthly decline since December 2002). This reversal in sentiment can also be seen through the lens of retail flows across baskets of semiconductor and bank names via Nasdaq Data Link’s U.S. Retail Equities Flow (UREF) dataset. Figure 6 shows the difference in retail buying of semi and bank stocks. Based on UREF data, retail investors began to favor semis relative to banks beginning in December 2023, with this net buying activity peaking in May 2025. Semi retail net buying activity continued to be net positive until July 2026 after which it has turned net negative amidst the sell-off in semis—further illustrating the shift in sentiment and speaking to the recent market rotation. Figure 5: Reversal in semis vs. banks speaks to the broadening of equity returns Figure 6: Mirrored reversal in semi vs. bank net dollar retail flows Source: Bloomberg. As of August 28, 2026. Source: Nasdaq Data Link . As of August 28, 2026. Includes semiconductors, semiconductor equipment and materials, and diversified and regional banks. Dollar volumes shown in “current day” dollars, deflated by the change in total U.S.-listed stock market capitalization to facilitate long-horizon comparisons. Following the iShares MSCI U.S. Momentum ETF (MTUM) returning a staggering 42.9% in Q2 2026—its largest quarterly return on record going back to 2013—per Figure 7, it has notably retrenched relative to the iShares MSCI U.S. Quality ETF (QUAL). While still higher by 20% YTD as of August 31 st , with MTUM’s top four names being AI stalwarts and comprising 20% of the ETF’s weight, and semis accounting for over 35% of the ETF’s weight, MTUM has sold off as investors have rotated into other parts of the market. When the quality factor outperforms, it can be a signal that investors are favoring corporate characteristics such as earnings durability, balance sheet strength, and low financial leverage amidst a volatile macro backdrop, Fed policy uncertainties, questions around AI capex, and an elevated financing environment. Figure 7: Momentum has sold off while the quality factor has come more into favor Source: Bloomberg. As of August 28, 2026. Solid corporate fundamentals, but watching for slowing earnings growth expectations Market gyrations are typically important to monitor for investor read throughs. But when investing for the longer-term, corporate fundamentals tend to be the driver of equity returns and broader risk taking. Following the outsized, AI-driven S&P 500 earnings growth in Q2, EPS growth is expected to remain very strong over the next three quarters—even if moderating from lofty levels (Figure 8). Likewise, S&P 500 sales growth is expected to be at least 10% YoY through Q1 2027. However, as the base effect becomes more challenging heading into mid-2027, these growth expectations bear watching in terms of a more material slowdown—albeit from very elevated levels. Another key proxy for the health of U.S. corporate fundamentals are credit spreads. The strong corporate earnings dynamics are also expressed via fixed income markets with both high yield and investment grade credit spreads hovering near their tightest levels since mid-2007 (Figure 9). It is worth noting that tech issuance is making up greater portions of the credit market—40% of 15-year-plus investment grade issuance in 2026 has come from companies related to the AI buildout, per Goldman Sachs. Across the pond, the hyperscalers alone comprised over 5% of Euro-denominated IG issuance YTD, per the ECB. On top of the angst around higher rates and AI capex questions, September tends to be the weakest month for U.S. equities historically with an average return of -0.2% since 1945 (Figure 10). The higher rates dynamic coupled with the historical volatility ahead of November U.S. mid-term elections (per our prior report ), could keep market sentiment fragile in the very near-term. title: Second-Quarter Earnings Show Breadth
author: Phil Mackintosh
description: 2026's market rally isn't just AI. Q2 earnings growth hit multi-year highs across chips, large caps, and beyond — with P/E multiples actually falling.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways AI Trade Rotation: From hyperscalers to chipmakers in the "picks-and-shovels" trade. SOX™ Fundamentals-Driven Rally: ~60% YTD price gain matched by ~60% earnings growth; 75% more projected next year. Nasdaq-100® Earnings Breadth at 4½-Year High: Over half of constituents with 20%+ growth; Q2 earnings near 80% p.a. — strongest since 2010. Large-Cap Valuations Compressing: Forward earnings outpacing price returns; P/E multiples falling despite record highs. Broader Than AI: Mid/small caps pricing in recovery on rate cuts, cooling wages, and tax tailwinds — strength extends well beyond chips. For markets, the artificial intelligence (AI) trade has been the dominant theme for the last couple of years. But it has shifted this year. Last year's story was about the AI hyperscalers – the handful of mega-cap tech companies spending hundreds of billions to build out AI infrastructure. This year, investors have rotated one step back in the supply chain. The "picks-and-shovels" trade is here, and chipmakers are the biggest beneficiaries. One constant, though, is that there’s been strong earnings growth underpinning this AI trade all along. In fact, the earnings strength we’ve seen in the AI hyperscalers and now chipmakers is accompanied by a broad-based strength across U.S. equities this year and in second-quarter earnings. SOX semis index sees price return and earnings moving in lockstep A key measure of chips stocks is the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index™ (SOX™), and it’s up about 60% year-to-date. That's a remarkable number. But what's more remarkable is what's behind it. SOX™ earnings are up over 60% this year (in just two quarters) – roughly in line with the price gain. And analysts project another 75% earnings growth by the end of next year. So, it’s been fundamentals driving this rally. Chart 1: Chips stocks’ prices and earnings are both up about 60% this year That’s also the key difference from the dot-com bubble. In 1999, valuations were running well ahead of earnings (if there were any earnings). Now, earnings are supporting price gains. In fact, for many sectors this year (including the SOX™), price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples are actually falling as earnings rise faster than stock prices (Chart 3). Nasdaq-100® earnings breadth is at 4½-year high The attention on the chipmaker rally can obscure something worth highlighting — earnings growth in 2026 has become remarkably broad-based. As of the second quarter, over half of all Nasdaq-100® companies reported earnings growth of at least 20% per annum (p.a.). More than four in five reported positive earnings growth. Both are the highest readings since the fourth quarter of 2021 — going back to the early post-Covid recovery. This breadth has helped push Nasdaq-100® earnings growth near 80% p.a. in the second quarter — its strongest earnings growth since 2010, when companies were recovering from the depths of the global financial crisis. Chart 2: Earnings breadth pushing Nasdaq-100® near 80% p.a. earnings growth Of course, there are some special circumstances here, with earnings boosted by tariff refunds and marking to market holdings in private companies like Anthropic. Still, even without these factors, large-cap earnings are robust. For large caps, earnings are outpacing returns With the SOX™, the Nasdaq-100® and the S&P 500 all near record highs, it's natural to wonder whether valuations are getting stretched. The data says no — in fact, they’re compressing. Across the major large-cap indexes, forward earnings growth has been outpacing price returns year-to-date. That means P/E multiples are falling as earnings climb faster than prices. That's true for the hyperscalers, the chipmakers, and the broader Nasdaq-100® and S&P 500. Chart 3: Large-cap earnings outpacing price growth, compressing PEs For mid and small caps, markets are betting on stronger earnings The valuation story is a little different once you move down the market cap spectrum. For mid caps (S&P 400), P/E multiples are flat year-to-date. For small caps (S&P 600), they're up nearly 5%. In other words, prices have been rising in line with or a bit faster than earnings for these groups – at most, a modest degree of multiple expansion. Multiple expansion, when it's modest, often reflects investors pricing in expected earnings improvement rather than paying for growth that has already arrived. And there are good reasons to expect it. Earlier rate cuts are feeding through to smaller companies, which carry more floating-rate debt than their large-cap peers. Wage growth is cooling. Tax tailwinds are flowing through to corporate earnings. Market’s strength goes well beyond chips and AI So, what do we make of all this? The SOX™ is the latest headline act and the earnings behind it are real. But framing 2026 as purely a chips or AI story misses most of the picture. The broader market resilience reflects macro tailwinds doing serious work. That combination has lifted a far wider set of companies than the headlines suggest.

title: Treasury hits Russia's VTB Bank with new sanctions over Iran ties
description: The new Russian bank sanctions follow a small handful of other actions that the Trump administration has taken since vowing to inflict "economic D-Day" on Iran.
content: A photo shows an exterior view of a branch of Russia's VTB Bank, on May 23, 2023 in Tehran, Iran. Fatemeh Bahrami | Anadolu Agency | Getty Images The Treasury Department on Monday announced new sanctions on Russia's state-controlled VTB Bank as part of its effort to economically isolate Iran by targeting its business partners and other financial "enablers." The action, which followed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's promise that a "large bank" would be sanctioned on Monday, was the latest penalty to be doled out as part of "Operation Economic Outcast," the Trump administration's non-military warfare strategy against Iran. The new sanctions against VTB Bank Public Joint Stock Company, Russia's second-largest bank, stemmed from allegations that it helped Tehran evade sanctions in part by "establishing correspondent relationships with sanctioned Iranian banks." The new financial action, which Treasury expects to block at least tens of millions of dollars, makes VTB "among the most comprehensively sanctioned financial institutions in the world," Treasury said in a press release . That's because the bank was already sanctioned by the U.S. in 2022 and early 2025 under the Biden administration. But curbing the bank may indirectly lead to economic limits on China, which is the top buyer of Iran's oil. Some observers were quick to raise questions about how much of an impact the new sanctions would have. "We're still digesting it a little bit," Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research, told CNBC following Treasury's announcement. While VTB is a large bank in Russia, it has already been significantly sanctioned, Marcus noted. "The devil does tend to be in the details," he said. "Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise," Bessent said in a statement. "Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers." Monday's action follows a small handful of other sanctions the Trump administration has imposed since last month, when it vowed to unleash "economic D-Day" on Iran and hobble its regime through global economic pressure. title: Counting the votes: Warsh faces a tough battle as the Fed girds for expected interest rate hike
description: Traders were pricing in a better than 92% probability of a rate increase, as well as a more than 75% chance for another one in December.
content: Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a news conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty Images Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh faces a tricky head count this week when he and his fellow policymakers decide on both the immediate and future path of interest rates. While markets have honed in on a near-certain quarter percentage point hike in Wednesday's vote, it's not at all clear how broad will be the margin among the 12 Federal Open Market Committee voters. Moreover, Warsh will have to decide how to message the move: Will this be the rare one-and-done on hikes, will there be more to come or will the chair maintain his cryptic posture in not trying to guide markets one way or the other? "With the market priced this way, it would be shocking if he came in and did nothing," Bill Dudley, the former New York Fed president, said in a CNBC interview. "It would really damage his credibility because it would basically be all talk, no action." Indeed, as of Monday afternoon, futures traders were pricing in a better than 92% probability of a rate increase this week, as well as a more than 75% chance that the FOMC would follow up in December with another move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Fed funds, the benchmark overnight borrowing rate, currently stand at 3.50% to 3.75%. The greater probabilities follow another run-up in fuel prices and inflation data last wee k that showed prices continued to climb in August. Both trends followed Warsh's comments a few weeks ago that the Fed would be forced into action unless there are more concrete signs that inflation is easing back to the central bank's 2% target. However, there are substantial complications. Wait or act? For one thing, the Fed historically has looked through the type of trends that are fueling inflation now. Economists generally agree that much of this year's increase has come from tariffs and an energy supply shock from the Iran war, both of which have uncertain impacts on the long-range trajectory of inflation. "We do not see a strong economic case for raising the funds rate," Goldman Sachs economist David Mericle said in a client note. "We think that all of the overshoot of 2% can be attributed to one-time factors whose impact is likely to fade." Nevertheless, Goldman changed its call from no change at this week's meeting to a hike, primarily because the firm's economists think the market expectations will force the Fed to move. Whether that also will be the case on an FOMC that voted 9-3 in favor of a hold at the July meeting is another matter. The three dissenters — regional presidents Lorie Logan of Dallas, Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis — all supported a quarter-point hike two months ago, when the Fed last met. Assuming their positions haven't changed, and there's been nothing in their public comments to suggest they have, that would mean four other members would have to switch their votes from hold to hike. Arguably the most-watched voter is Governor Christopher Waller. In public remarks delivered Sept. 3, Waller voiced suppor t for another hold at this meeting, albeit with the usual caveats about watching data to confirm that disinflation trends are continuing. Mostly, he merely urged patience rather than a rush to hike. "What's the cost of waiting one meeting? Hiking 25 basis points, one meeting right now, is not going to bring the [consumer price index] down to 2%," he said. The CPI for August actually showed headline inflation running at a 3.4% rate, though the core rate, which excludes food and soaring energy costs, was a more benign 2.4%, down 0.1 percentage point from July. Waller wasn't alone in advocating patience — New York Fed President John Williams told CNBC less than two weeks ago that a "wait-and-see" approach seems to make sense. Earlier in the summer, Williams, whose perch atop the New York Fed is traditionally considered part of the influential "troika" of influence at the central bank, said he thinks inflation has peaked . Also in recent remarks, Governor Michael Barr expressed concern about temporary inflation taking deeper hold and said he would be open to a hike, not set on one. The FOMC breakdown So who would join the three July dissenters? Warsh is largely expected to be part of the hiking group, considering his remarks in Jackson Hole, Wyoming last month. Governor Lisa Cook said in early August that she's "prepared to act" to take on inflation. Conversely, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson and Chicago's Austan Goolsbee also have counseled a more patient approach. That would leave Governors Philip Jefferson, who is the vice chair; Jerome Powell , the former chair, who has kept a decidedly low profile since stepping down from the top spot, and Michelle Bowman, who spoke little on monetary policy over the summer and whose last related remarks were in May, when she also expressed concern about hiking unnecessarily. Then there's a larger wildcard: Should Warsh press the case for a hike, would those on the fence simply cross over to his side in the interest of presenting a united front? The vote margin not only will reveal the extent of the intellectual divide on the committee between those who think inflation is temporary and those who believe price pressures are becoming entrenched. It also will provide important signals about how effectively Warsh's leadership is reverberating inside the Fed. "It should be noted that, if the Fed does indeed raise rates this week, it may not look, in retrospect, like a close call," David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, said in his weekly market note. "If a majority within the committee coalesces around a decision to hike, the other members may well join them to portray a more united front to the public and the President." In such a case, Kelly said the final vote could see two, one or no dissents. From there, markets will look at the Fed's "dot plot" update. The grid spells out, anonymously, the rate expectations for the full 19 participants at the meeting, though Warsh withheld his dot for the June update. Investors will look for how much conviction there will be for two hikes this year, as well as the outlook for 2027. This will also feature the first look at 2029. The Fed almost never hikes or cuts just once but rather moves in cycles, as policymakers view incremental one-off moves as ineffective. A 10-8 split in favor of one hike — assuming Warsh's disdain for forward guidance and nonparticipation in the update — would indicate that "some participants might be ambivalent about the first hike and some might want to avoid pushing market expectations any higher," Mericle wrote. "But we see a risk of a majority for two hikes if more participants than we expect see a hike this week as a normal response to higher oil prices and AI demand and the start of a series of rate hikes," he added. In the case of a close divide on the committee, attention then will turn to Warsh's news conference Wednesday afternoon, and how the chair conveys FOMC sentiment. Dudley, the former New York Fed chief, said "the Fed needs to explain how they're thinking about the economy." "Now [Warsh has] just got to follow that up with action," Dudley said. "If he does that, I think he's basically fixed the problem that he created in his first two press conferences." title: The stock market could do something strange this week after the Fed decision
description: Odds of more interest rate hikes coming this year have grown.
content: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Sept. 8, 2026. Brendan McDermid | Reuters This week, the stock market could do something unusual: rally on a rate hike. Wall Street is expecting that the Federal Reserve will raise rates this week after Chairman Kevin Warsh 's tough speech against inflation at Jackson Hole last month was followed by a series of hot inflation reports , a spike in oil prices and a surge in expectations for a quarter-point increase. The market is now pricing in a 90% likelihood that the federal funds rate — which serves as a baseline for other borrowing costs such as mortgages — will rise 3.75% to 4.00% following Wednesday's decision, according to the CME FedWatch Tool . The probability of two more increases coming, in October and December, have also spiked, fed funds futures pricing shows. What's unusual, however, is the possibility that the stock market could actually rise in that scenario, which the major averages treated as positive on Friday . Typically, stocks fall on the prospect of higher rates because they raise borrowing costs and lower the value of future earnings. But the prospect of worsening inflation, and the upward pressure that is adding to longer-dated Treasury yields, has traders shifting their priorities to the bond market first. "It's the signaling impact and the net impact on the long end of the curve that would end up being the positive thing for equity markets," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer at Horizon. "That's the unusual setup today." Investors are hoping a rate hike or two from the Fed will tame pricing pressures and keep long-term bond yields anchored. On Monday, the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5% for the first time since 2023, a development that also hurt equities. The major averages were down across the board at that same time. Dovish or hawkish hike? Part of the market reaction may come down to which Warsh shows up at the press conference: the July Fed chief who was vague about the central bank's commitment to tackling inflation, or the Jackson Hole leader who was clear the Fed will do whatever it could do bring inflation down. If the Fed chair continues to sound tough against inflation, and restores credibility, as he did in August at the Wyoming gathering, the market may immediately pull forward rate expectations. Bank of America Securities' rates strategist Mark Cabana said he expects 2-year Treasury yields would rise 5 to 10 basis points, while the 30-year rates fall just as much. But a dovish press conference in which Warsh implies the hike was unpopular, or that only a few hikes will follow, may confuse investors and send longer-dated bond yields higher. Cabana said he expects 2-year yields to fall by 5 basis points, and 30-year rates to rise by 5 basis points in this scenario. "Fed faces simple choice at Sept FOMC: hike or risk large bond spike," Cabana wrote. "If the Fed does not hike with current pricing, it risks a sharp and disorderly [U.S. Treasury] long end move." Stock reaction Typically, the start of a new hiking cycle is a bad sign for stocks. A look at the S&P 500 following the initial rate hikes of six tightening cycles over the last 30-plus years showed that the broader index drops immediately in the month afterward, losing an average 3.4%, according to Canaccord Genuity analyst Michael Graham. Over the following two to three months, the S&P 500 continues to perform poorly, though the results over the longer term start to improve, the analyst said. However, if the Fed is able to restore confidence in its commitment to tackling inflation, it could relieve some of the pressure in the bond market, which could then also relieve stocks. JPMorgan's Mislav Matejka said he expects that much of the normalization of bond yields is already behind investors, which could clear the way for further upside for equities through the end of the year. "Much of the repricing has reflected the rebuilding of a previously compressed term premium, not a signal that inflation is about to spiral," Matejka wrote. title: Trump agrees to ethics requirements in crypto Clarity Act as GOP seeks Democratic votes
description: Community banks fear customers will withdraw deposits to buy stablecoin crypto assets that could pay higher yields.
content: Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., is seen in the U.S. Capitol on Oct. 16, 2025. Tom Williams | CQ-Roll Call, Inc. | Getty Images President Donald Trump agreed to support some new ethics restrictions in long-awaited crypto market structure legislation set for a preliminary Senate vote on Tuesday. But it remains unclear whether the measure, known as the Clarity Act , has enough votes to advance in the Senate as last-minute lobbying by banks and the cryptocurrency industry intensifies. The Clarity Act , which would establish a new regulatory structure for cryptocurrencies and other digital assets, has languished in the Senate for months. The bill cleared the Senate Banking Committee in May, but has stalled as Senate leaders have struggled to wrangle the 60 votes needed for approval. With full attendance, at least seven Democrats would need to support the measure to escape the filibuster. A range of issues have slowed the process and could put the outcome of Tuesday's vote, which would end debate and allow the Senate to begin moving toward passage, in doubt. Banks warn they cannot support the bill unless it includes a fix to stop interest-like payments on stablecoins, which they say could cause customers to pull deposits and place them in high-yield crypto accounts. And Democrats, only two of whom voted to advance the bill out of committee, have said they cannot support the bill unless it includes stronger ethics language to prevent Trump, his family and officials from profiting from crypto ventures. Republican leaders on the bill released an update to the measure late Sunday that they say reflects their final offer to meet Democratic demands. The updated text includes what the Republicans say represents large parts of a crypto ethics agreement brokered by Sens. Thom Tillis , R-N.C., and Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., that Trump has now agreed to. That includes a key Democratic ask to allow state attorneys general to enforce ethics requirements on federal officials. The bill now also includes a compromise on stablecoin yield aimed at appeasing banking interests by directing the Treasury secretary to restrict rewards if deposit flight from community banks occurs on a substantial scale. What happens if Warsh wavers Hassett kept up to $5 million Coinbase stake as Trump reshaped crypto policy Trump's energy holdings have surged as the Iran war moved oil markets Tuesday's preliminary vote is a put-up-or-shut-up moment for the crypto bill. Supporters are hopeful they can scrape enough support to keep the bill alive. Sen. Cynthia Lummis , R-Wyo., one of the leaders of the bill, in a statement after releasing the updated legislation, said, "This text is truly bipartisan and includes more than 120 of Democrats' demands. "A no vote on Tuesday means opposing real ethics reforms on politicians' personal investments, handing American leadership in digital assets to our foreign competitors, and leaving Americans with zero protections in the digital asset markets," Lummis said. "Democrats got what they wanted; now they need to take yes for an answer." Many Democrats oppose the bill, largely because of the lack of ethics language they say must address Trump and his family's profiting off of crypto ventures. "I can assure you that I'm not hearing from my constituents that their No. 1 concern is to pass the Clarity Act," Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a Sunday video on X. "This is a bill that is masquerading as a way to create good regulation and protection for consumers with respect to cryptocurrency, but it has some big problems that have not been fixed," Van Hollen said. Van Hollen said in his post that "We can't let this pass." Still, the Clarity Act appears to be a jump ball at this point. A Democratic aide familiar with the negotiations said when it comes time for the preliminary vote, enough Democrats may support keeping the bill alive. The aide, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss private negotiations, said Senate Majority Leader John Thune , R-S.D., has pitched the vote as a "free vote," meaning that the vote is merely to keep the bill moving and the measure will be amended and voted on again before final passage to address lingering concerns. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, one of the leaders of the bill who was financially backed by crypto interests during his 2024 campaign to oust former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, tried to remind senators on Sunday that Tuesday is not the final vote. "This is not a vote on final passage. It is a vote to end debate on whether the United States Senate should even consider a bill to regulate digital assets," Moreno said in an X post . "If Senators have concerns about the bill, they can offer an amendment after we agree to take it up." The White House has also teased further concessions on ethics language and other issues, but only if the Senate clears the preliminary vote, the Democratic aide said. That promise could act as an additional sweetener to entice crypto-curious Democrats to vote to advance the bill to see what the White House will offer. "The President has been unequivocal: Congress must pass the CLARITY Act so we can stay ahead of foreign competitors and lead the world in innovation," the White House press office said in an emailed statement, without answering CNBC's questions about its concessions on Clarity Act ethics language. "The Trump Administration has worked tirelessly with Congress on the CLARITY Act and has already agreed to the most comprehensive and wide-ranging ethics provision in history." Crypto interests are bullish about the bill's prospects. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, whose company has been out front about supporting the bill, said on CNBC on Thursday that the legislation is ready to be supported by the Senate. Armstrong also said regulation will be coming for crypto regardless of the vote tally. "Frankly, if it doesn't pass, it's also going to be a good outcome because the SEC and the CFTC have said that they're ready to publish rulemaking, and we're going to get regulatory clarity one way or another on the 15th or the day or two after," he said, referring to the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Coinbase also struck an agreement with financial services provider Moov last week to grant community banks access to stablecoin capabilities, a move likely intended to ease community bank fears of being bigfooted by the Clarity Act. CNBC was first to report the agreement. Banks, including the Independent Community Bankers of America, the trade association for community banks, have led opposition to the Clarity Act, including the latest version that adds new authority for Treasury to crack down on stablecoin rewards if deposit flight occurs. "Additionally, the inclusion of a deposit-flight 'circuit breaker' is an acknowledgment that shifting deposits from regulated financial institutions into payment stablecoins can threaten credit availability and create broader economic consequences," ICBA wrote along with seven other banking associations in a Monday letter. "However, a circuit breaker that activates only after substantial deposit flight has already occurred is not a safeguard at all." "Further technical refinements are needed to ensure that the text clearly and directly prohibits interest-like payments on payment stablecoins," the groups wrote. While the bill could technically be brought back in an amended form if the preliminary vote Tuesday fails, it's unclear whether lawmakers have enough time to amend the package and get it across the finish line before the end of this Congress should Tuesday's vote fail. In a statement to CNBC, Brooke Ybarra, senior vice president for innovation and strategy at the American Bankers Association, said, "bankers across the country have had the chance to speak with their senators about the importance of preserving the deposits that support local lending." Ybarra also sounded optimistic that senators will oppose the bill when it comes to the floor. "We appreciate the growing number of lawmakers who share our concerns with the current interest loophole in the bill and recognize that targeted changes to the Clarity Act can strengthen the legislation and improve its chances of clearing the full Senate," Ybarra said. "We remain optimistic that the Senate will ultimately consider an improved Clarity Act that embraces innovation without undermining the economy." title: Novo CEO tells CNBC why drugmaker is rebranding, needs to 'rethink' obesity strategy

content: In this article NVO NVO Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 19:02 19:02 Novo CEO talks about rebrand, corporate changes amid fight for obesity market share News Videos Novo Nordisk on Monday said it is rebranding its name to "Novo" and updating its corporate culture, as the company works to win back market share in the obesity drug space. The Danish drugmaker called the changes the beginning of a new chapter, as it has been grappling with stiff competition from chief rival Eli Lilly and investor pressure to deliver new blockbuster products and chart a path toward long-term growth. Novo is preparing to detail its business strategy changes during its Capital Markets Day event on Sept. 21. In an exclusive interview with CNBC, Novo CEO Mike Doustdar said the rebrand and culture shift are "part of the same package" for the company to evolve its strategy as it tries to win back customers from Lilly. "I think there's no secret that over the last four or five years, the external environment and what has happened to Novo Nordisk has really made us reflect how we need to readjust and rethink about the next decade to come and what shifts are needed in our strategic direction," he told CNBC. Doustdar said the "work is cut out for us," adding that Novo needs to improve several aspects – from research and development and manufacturing to sales and marketing – to be able to compete in the obesity drug market. Courtesy: Novo Nordisk Shares of Novo have dropped about 15% this year despite the successful launch of the oral version of Wegovy, which surpassed 3 million prescriptions as of June. The company recently scrapped three trials on an experimental cardiovascular drug. That challenge came as it continues to lag in the obesity space with 38.8% market share compared to Lilly's 60.9% in the second quarter, according to a Lilly earnings presentation citing IQVIA data. In a release, Novo also announced a broader company rebrand focused around the phrase "Lasting Health Starts Now," which promotes the idea that patients should make progress toward long-term well-being immediately rather than later. The company said the marketing is a bid to build relevance and trust with the public and other stakeholders, and bring "breakthrough science closer to people's daily lives." When asked whether the rebrand and cultural overhaul were driven by Novo's recent market share losses in obesity, Doustdar said the changes were less about competitive setbacks and more about adapting to a dramatically different operating environment. Novo Nordisk CEO Maziar Mike Doustdar waits for the start of the pharmaceutical company’s annual general meeting in Copenhagen, Denmark, March 26, 2026. Tom Little | Reuters He said the rapid growth of obesity treatments has transformed Novo's patient base and shifted the market toward a more consumer-oriented model, where patients move on and off therapies more frequently than in traditional diabetes care. As a result, Doustdar said Novo needs to become more focused on meeting patients where they are, while increasing the speed and clarity of its decision-making to keep pace with the evolving market. "Our operating environment phenomenally changed compared to just 10 years ago," he told CNBC. Novo Nordisk will remain the legal name for the company, according to the release. That original name dates back to the 1989 merger of two competing Danish pharmaceutical companies: Novo Terapeutisk Laboratorium and Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium. The drugmaker said its corporate culture will be based on a new set of four principles that will help it gain advantages in an increasingly competitive market where more of its products have gone direct-to-consumer. Those tenets are innovating with patients as the primary focus, raising the company's performance to "create greater value for all stakeholders," setting clearer priorities and simpler workflows and never compromising on patient safety and ethics. "When you think about strategy, that's really the the journey you're taking and the direction you're setting the company to go forward with," Doustdar said. "But you also need behaviors. You need a cultural element that allows your colleagues and yourself to really make sure that a strategy gets executed." Despite its challenges, Novo has had one significant tailwind this year in the launch of the oral version of Wegovy. On top of its explosive launch, the pill had a head start over a rival weight loss pill from Lilly called Foundayo. Doustdar said Novo has maintained "a lion's share" of the oral market even with competition, noting that physicians find the Wegovy pill to be more effective than Lilly's, with around 17% of weight loss.
